md: A **monomer** is a small molecule that can join to others like it. A **polymer** is the very long chain molecule made when thousands of monomers join. The process is **addition polymerisation**: *addition* because the monomers simply add on to one another and nothing else is made, *polymerisation* because a polymer is the result. Each word earns a mark.

title: Before you watch
md: This clip is made for a separate Chemistry course. If it moves on to condensation polymers, natural polymers or recycling, none of that is on your specification.

explain: The monomers add on to one another and a polymer is what forms, so the process is addition polymerisation. Polymerisation on its own earns one of the two marks; addition is the other.

md: When one of the two bonds in a C=C opens, each carbon is left with a bond to spare, and that bond links it to the next monomer. That is why every monomer for addition polymerisation is an **alkene**, or has a C=C like one. An alkane's bonds are all single and all in use, so it has nothing to open and **cannot** form an addition polymer.

title: Why nothing else is made
md: The monomers only add on to one another: no atom leaves and no second product forms. Section 6 turns that into a check you can run on every repeat unit you draw.

prompt: Ethene and ethane both have two carbon atoms. Why can ethene form an addition polymer when ethane cannot?
options: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
ethene has more hydrogen atoms to give away
ethane molecules are too large to join together
answer: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
explain: Compare the two drawings: ethene's carbons share two bonds, ethane's share one, and every other bond on ethane is taken by a hydrogen. Opening one bond of the C=C gives each carbon a spare bond to link with, which is the C=C answer.

text: 3. Naming a polymer from its monomer

md:
Build the polymer's name from the monomer's: **poly**, then the monomer's name **in brackets**.
**Ethene** → **poly(ethene)**; the scheme also accepts polythene.
**Propene** → **poly(propene)**.
**Backwards:** the monomer is the name inside the brackets.

The other monomer CCEA names is **chloroethene**, once called vinyl chloride, whose polymer is sold as **PVC**. Poly(ethene) makes carrier bags and cling film; PVC makes window frames and drainpipes. When a question says name, write the chemical name, not the trade name.

title: One rule, one mark
md: Summer 2025's C2 Foundation report: most candidates could not name the polymer made from ethene, and many left the line blank. It is a rule to learn, not chemistry to work out.

Name the polymer made from the monomer chloroethene.
explain: The rule works the same way for every monomer: poly, then the monomer's name in brackets. Ethene gave poly(ethene), so chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene). PVC is the name on the shop label, not the one a question asks for.

md: A polymer is too long to draw, so you draw one **repeat unit**: the part that repeats all along the chain. It shows two carbons joined by a **single** bond, because the C=C has opened; every group each carbon had in the monomer; a **bond through each square bracket**, because the chain carries on; and **n** after the closing bracket, because the unit repeats a large number of times.
Every carbon still makes **four bonds**. Count them on the drawing above: two to hydrogens, one to the other carbon, and one through the bracket to the next unit.

prompt: In the repeat unit of poly(ethene) drawn above, count the bonds around one carbon atom, including the bond that passes through the bracket. How many are there?
explain: Count them on the drawing: two to hydrogens, one to the other carbon and one through the bracket, which makes four, as carbon always has. A drawing that kept the double bond would give each carbon five, which is how that mistake gets caught.

md:
**The question.** Show chloroethene forming its polymer as a structural equation. **[2]**
**Step 1.** Draw chloroethene with its C=C, and write **n** in front: n molecules go in.
**Step 2.** Draw the two carbons again, now joined by a **single** bond, with the Cl and the three H exactly where they were.

**Step 3.** Add a bond out of each carbon, through a square bracket on each side.
**Step 4.** Write **n** after the closing bracket. One mark is for the structure and one for n on both sides of the arrow.
**Step 5.** Check: four bonds at every carbon.

prompt: In the structural equation for chloroethene drawn above, which part of the drawing shows that the chain carries on beyond the repeat unit?
options: the bonds passing through the brackets
the n in front of the chloroethene
the Cl atom on the first carbon
answer: the bonds passing through the brackets
explain: A bracket marks where one unit ends; a bond crossing it says the chain does not stop there. The n counts how many units there are, but it is the bonds through the brackets that show the chain carrying on.

md:
**1.** In addition polymerisation the monomers only add on: there is no second product.
**2.** So no atom leaves the chain.
**3.** Each monomer becomes one repeat unit.
**4.** So a repeat unit has **exactly the atoms of one monomer**, only rebonded.
**5.** So it has the monomer's relative formula mass too.

Take ethene: $\ce{C2H4}$ goes in, and every repeat unit of poly(ethene) is $\ce{C2H4}$ as well, with Mr 28 both times. Check every repeat unit you draw twice: the **same atoms** as the monomer, and **four bonds** at every carbon.

prompt: The repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) is drawn on the right of the figure above. How many hydrogen atoms does it contain?
explain: Count the H labels round the two carbons of the repeat unit: 3. Chloroethene on the left has 3 as well, because the chlorine took the place of one of ethene's four hydrogens and nothing was lost when the monomers joined.

prompt: Working back from a section of polymer chain to its monomer, what is the last step?
options: put the C=C back between the two carbons of the unit
remove the bonds that join the unit to its neighbours
mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
answer: put the C=C back between the two carbons of the unit
explain: The order is mark off two carbons, remove the outer bonds, then put the double bond back. The last step is the one most often left out, and without it the answer is an alkane, which cannot polymerise.

md:
**Step 1.** The pattern repeats every two carbons: one carbon with two H, the next with one H and a $\ce{CH3}$.
**Step 2.** Cut out one unit and remove its two outer bonds.
**Step 3.** Put the C=C back between the two chain carbons, with the $\ce{CH3}$ still hanging from the second.
**Step 4.** Count every carbon, the one in $\ce{CH3}$ included, and name the alkene with that many.

prompt: In the polymer chain drawn above, every second carbon carries a CH₃ group. Name the monomer the chain was made from.
explain: Put the double bond back into one two-carbon unit and count: two carbons in the chain and one in the CH₃ make three, with a C=C, so the monomer is propene. Propane has no double bond, so it could never have polymerised.

prompt: Tetrafluoroethene, C₂F₄, has a C=C with two fluorine atoms on each carbon. What goes between the two carbons of its repeat unit?
options: a single bond, with two F on each carbon
a double bond, with two F on each carbon
a single bond, with one F on each carbon
answer: a single bond, with two F on each carbon
explain: The rule is the same for any monomer: one bond of the C=C opens, so the carbons are left joined by a single bond, and every group stays where it was. Two F on each carbon in the monomer means two F on each carbon in the unit.

md: **A long section of chain** (2022). Six carbons are printed, but one repeat unit is still two carbons, because each monomer brought two.
**Two names, two marks** (2022, 2025). The process is worth two marks, addition and polymerisation; the polymer's name is worth one.

prompt: A section of an addition polymer printed in a question shows six carbon atoms in its chain. How many of those chain carbons make up one repeat unit?
explain: Each monomer's C=C brought two carbons into the chain, so the pattern repeats every two carbons, however long the printed section is. Six chain carbons are three repeat units.

md: The hardest shape is a monomer with a group of several atoms, such as propene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH3}$. Only the **two carbons of the C=C** go into the chain; the $\ce{CH3}$ hangs off its carbon, as in the monomer. Three carbons in a row inside the brackets loses the mark.

**Step 1.** The C=C's two carbons make the chain.
**Step 2.** A single bond between them: H and H on the first, H and $\ce{CH3}$ on the second.
**Step 3.** A bond through each bracket; n after.
**Check.** $\ce{C3H6}$, the atoms of propene.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Condensation polymers, natural polymers such as proteins and DNA, and plastics recycling are not on the CCEA Double Award specification.

prompt: But-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, forms an addition polymer. How many carbon atoms of each repeat unit sit in the main chain, inside the brackets?
explain: Only the two carbons of the C=C join the chain, as in the poly(propene) unit above. The CH₂CH₃ group is a side group hanging off the second carbon, so two carbons are in the chain and two hang off it.

md:
Name the process, **addition polymerisation**, and any polymer: poly(monomer).
Draw a repeat unit: a **single** C–C bond, a bond through each **bracket**, **n**; n on both sides of the equation.
Check it: the **same atoms** as the monomer, four bonds at every carbon.
Work back from a chain to its monomer by putting the **C=C** back.
Keep a side group off the chain, whatever the monomer.

Polymers sit inside the organic question of the C2 paper. The first marks are names: the process, or the polymer from its monomer. At Higher the last marks are a drawing: a repeat unit, a structural equation with n on both sides, or a monomer from a section of chain. Stuck? Draw the monomer, open its double bond, count four bonds at every carbon. The Sheet lists the traps.
